video_title: Live at Univ. of Oregon: AI and State Governments with Nik Blosser
gist: Oregon Chief AI Officer Nik Blosser describes running an unbudgeted, non-statutory state AI office built on risk-tiered 'boring competency' governance, illustrated by a Medicaid/SNAP chatbot that went from 70% to 95% answer coverage and then to a public-facing version. He reports frontier labs have hit the limit of voluntary transparency (one refused to share its third-party evaluator contract) as Oregon drafts rules to buy only independently reviewed frontier AI, and pitches Oregon's semiconductor and robotics base as an AI-safety hub.

themes.theme: Oregon's Chief AI Officer role and constraints

insights.claim: Oregon's Chief AI Officer role has no dedicated budget and no statutory basis; it was created by the state CIO repurposing roles, forcing the officer to solicit resources from other departments.
insights.speaker: Nik Blosser (Oregon Chief AI Officer)
insights.so_what: State AI offices are under-resourced and fragile, limiting near-term state AI procurement scale.
insights.quote: I actually don't have a budget. I don't I don't have I'm not in the statute.

insights.claim: Oregon's governor created an AI task force by executive order in late 2023; its February 2025 report recommended appointing a state AI point person among roughly 40 other recommendations that did not align with Oregon's two-year budget cycle.
insights.speaker: Nik Blosser (Oregon Chief AI Officer)
insights.so_what: Biennial state budget cycles lag AI developments by years, slowing public-sector AI adoption.

insights.claim: Blosser argues that without a central AI office and comprehensive policy, state agency AI use would become a dangerous free-for-all.
insights.speaker: Nik Blosser (Oregon Chief AI Officer)
insights.so_what: Central governance offices are a prerequisite for, not a barrier to, state AI deployment.
insights.quote: If my office didn't exist, if there wasn't a comprehensive policy, I think you would have a free-for-all

insights.claim: States can currently recruit strong AI talent from the federal government, as Oregon did with a recent hire, reflecting federal workforce displacement.
insights.speaker: Nik Blosser (Oregon Chief AI Officer)
insights.so_what: Federal workforce cuts are a talent tailwind for state government tech capacity.
insights.quote: there's actually a lot of opportunity in hiring federal employees right now at the state level

insights.claim: State chief AI officers coordinate through the Center for Civic Futures (run by Cass Madison), which meets at least monthly, holds conferences and grants money to states for innovative AI ideas, and through the National Association of State CIOs.
insights.speaker: Nik Blosser (Oregon Chief AI Officer)
insights.so_what: Cross-state AI policy diffusion runs through a small number of networks, accelerating convergence of state standards.

insights.claim: Oregon triages agency AI proposals via an AI use form that flags higher risk if the system is public-facing, uses confidential/personal data, or performs any of ~20 'rights or safety impacting' functions such as employment, benefits decisions or bridge load analysis; data must reside and be processed in the United States.
insights.speaker: Nik Blosser (Oregon Chief AI Officer)
insights.so_what: Vendors selling to states need US data residency and clear internal-vs-public, data-sensitivity positioning to clear review quickly.

insights.claim: Almost all AI implementations approved so far by the state of Oregon have been lower risk, with only a couple of higher-risk systems approved.
insights.speaker: Nik Blosser (Oregon Chief AI Officer)
insights.so_what: State AI adoption is concentrated in low-risk internal tooling; high-risk public use cases remain rare.
insights.quote: almost all of the implementations so far have not been higher risk at the state of Oregon

insights.claim: Blosser frames Oregon's AI strategy under the mantra 'we aspire to boring competency', emphasizing crawl-walk-run deployment with extensive testing and monitoring to build employee and public trust.
insights.speaker: Nik Blosser (Oregon Chief AI Officer)
insights.so_what: Incremental, well-tested deployments are how public-sector AI demand will expand.

insights.claim: Blosser states AI should not be trusted to make government decisions at present, only to help humans make decisions.
insights.speaker: Nik Blosser (Oregon Chief AI Officer)
insights.so_what: Autonomous decision-making AI for benefits/eligibility is not a near-term state market; decision-support is.
insights.quote: we're a long way from having AI make any decisions. I don't trust that. No one should trust that right now.

insights.claim: Oregon's AI policy requires plain-language AI system transparency disclosures for public-facing tools covering ownership, function, data access, identified risks and mitigations, and where user-entered data is stored.
insights.speaker: Nik Blosser (Oregon Chief AI Officer)
insights.so_what: Public-facing government AI vendors must support detailed transparency documentation.

insights.claim: Blosser claims that roughly 80% of AI success depends on good data and, separately, 80% of secure AI depends on identity, topics legislators and agency leaders have historically undervalued.
insights.speaker: Nik Blosser (Oregon Chief AI Officer)
insights.so_what: Data infrastructure and identity management are the gating spend categories for government AI.
insights.quote: 80% of the ability for AI to be successful is good data. And the other 80% of secure AI is identity.

insights.claim: Oregon's health and human services developers built an internal chatbot for about 1,000 Medicaid/SNAP eligibility workers that answers policy questions with citations; it was piloted with 1, then 10, then 50 users before full release.
insights.speaker: Nik Blosser (Oregon Chief AI Officer)
insights.so_what: Staged rollout is the template for state AI deployments.

insights.claim: Oregon's internal Medicaid/SNAP policy chatbot answered about 70% of questions at launch and about 95% within three months after iterative knowledge-source updates.
insights.speaker: Nik Blosser (Oregon Chief AI Officer)
insights.so_what: Retrieval-based internal assistants can reach high coverage quickly with ongoing knowledge maintenance.
insights.quote: it was maybe could answer 70% of the questions. But then over time they had built in um a process of updating the the knowledge sources and within three months it was at answering 95%

insights.claim: Success of the internal chatbot led Oregon to launch, a couple of weeks before the recording, a higher-risk public-facing chatbot answering questions about Medicaid work requirements taking effect in January, with exhaustive testing and live monitoring.
insights.speaker: Nik Blosser (Oregon Chief AI Officer)
insights.so_what: Internal-to-external progression shows how state AI use expands once trust is earned; federal Medicaid work requirements are driving demand.

themes.theme: Frontier lab transparency and third-party evaluation

insights.claim: Oregon's governor charged Blosser with a 90-day report on how the state could purchase only frontier AI that has been third-party or independently reviewed, part of a wave of state laws and executive orders seeking such disclosure.
insights.speaker: Nik Blosser (Oregon Chief AI Officer)
insights.so_what: State procurement may soon condition frontier model purchases on independent evaluation, affecting lab sales to government.

insights.claim: Blosser reports significant information asymmetry between frontier labs and the public sector, and says labs initially engaged but have reached the limit of what they will do voluntarily.
insights.speaker: Nik Blosser (Oregon Chief AI Officer)
insights.so_what: Voluntary disclosure has plateaued, raising the odds of mandatory state disclosure rules.
insights.quote: have definitely reached the limit of what they're willing to do voluntarily

insights.claim: When Blosser asked a frontier lab to share its contract with a third-party evaluator to understand restrictions on what the evaluator could publish, the lab declined, leading him to question whether such reviews can be called independent.
insights.speaker: Nik Blosser (Oregon Chief AI Officer)
insights.so_what: 'Independent evaluation' claims by labs may not survive state procurement scrutiny.
insights.quote: I don't know how we can call anything independent or third-party reviewed if we don't even know that that this independent evaluator is restricted or free to say what's on their mind.

insights.claim: Blosser attributes lab behavior partly to IPO and public-market pressures, arguing the public sector therefore needs its own access and expertise to 'call balls and strikes' on AI risk.
insights.speaker: Nik Blosser (Oregon Chief AI Officer)
insights.so_what: Upcoming lab IPOs increase pressure for external government evaluation capacity.

insights.claim: Blosser splits AI assurance into two buckets: frontier intelligence (lab, pre-release testing, post-release monitoring) and AI systems that take actions or make decisions, including future robotics and autonomous driving, where states expect to focus third-party evaluation.
insights.speaker: Nik Blosser (Oregon Chief AI Officer)
insights.so_what: A market for third-party AI system evaluators (e.g., non-discrimination compliance) is emerging for state higher-risk deployments.

insights.claim: Blosser says there are now enough independent evaluators to assess AI systems for compliance with federal non-discrimination law, framing that bipartisanly rather than as 'woke AI'.
insights.speaker: Nik Blosser (Oregon Chief AI Officer)
insights.so_what: Compliance-framed AI audits can gain bipartisan state adoption.
insights.quote: You don't have to call it woke AI, you can just call it compliance with federal non-discrimination law and most states can agree to that.

insights.claim: Frazier argues AI talent is concentrated in San Francisco's 'Silicon Tower' and focused on frontier risks, leaving states without verifiers for mundane deployments like Medicaid eligibility.
insights.speaker: Kevin Frazier (host)
insights.so_what: There is an underserved market for deployment-specific, 'boring' AI verification.

themes.theme: Public trust and state data infrastructure

insights.claim: DHM Research polling of Oregonians found widespread opposition to data centers and unease about AI in sensitive contexts, with support rising when government AI is framed as improving services rather than efficiency/replacement.
insights.speaker: Kevin Frazier (host)
insights.so_what: Framing of government AI (service improvement vs. DOGE-style efficiency) materially shifts public acceptance.

insights.claim: Oregon's roughly 50,000 state employees hold views on AI ranging from wanting unrestricted use to wanting none, mirroring public polling.
insights.speaker: Nik Blosser (Oregon Chief AI Officer)
insights.so_what: Internal workforce sentiment is a key constraint on state AI rollout.

insights.claim: Frazier argues good state AI requires full-stack investment: personnel, machine-readable data, cross-actor data sharing and possibly third-party data contributions, noting examples like North Dakota making legislative materials machine-readable, Massachusetts' data hub and West Virginia improving data collection because models underperform in Appalachia.
insights.speaker: Kevin Frazier (host)
insights.so_what: State data modernization is a precondition and spending opportunity for government AI.

insights.claim: Frazier predicts running all laws through AI to find loopholes and typos, and simulating how laws could fail, will become table stakes in future legislative sessions.
insights.speaker: Kevin Frazier (host)
insights.so_what: Legislative AI tooling is a likely growth area.
insights.quote: I think that's going to be table stakes in in future legislative sessions.

insights.claim: Recoding America's 'deproceduralizer' tool has been used by New Jersey and Virginia to scan administrative rules and laws for regulatory cuts, with Maryland and Oregon evaluating it and a paper forthcoming.
insights.speaker: Nik Blosser (Oregon Chief AI Officer)
insights.so_what: AI-driven deregulation tooling is spreading across states.

insights.claim: Blosser claims Intel's Hillsboro and Beaverton, Oregon sites are the only advanced semiconductor foundry in North America, with others in Taiwan and Korea, and that the NSF recently awarded the region a grant for advanced semiconductor work.
insights.speaker: Nik Blosser (Oregon Chief AI Officer)
insights.so_what: Oregon's semiconductor R&D base underpins its pitch as an AI hub (claim is speaker's characterization).

insights.claim: Blosser says Oregon State University is the only US university offering PhDs in both robotics and AI, and cites Agility Robotics as a local robotics company.
insights.speaker: Nik Blosser (Oregon Chief AI Officer)
insights.so_what: Robotics talent cluster supports physical-AI company formation in Oregon.

insights.claim: Blosser is bullish on AI safety-related companies, including cybersecurity, growing in Oregon given its semiconductor base, universities, startup culture and location between Seattle and Silicon Valley.
insights.speaker: Nik Blosser (Oregon Chief AI Officer)
insights.so_what: Oregon may become a niche cluster for AI safety and security startups.
insights.quote: I'm actually pretty bullish on Oregon and companies that deal in what I would call AI safety.
